acknowledge.text: You can't quite settle. That's uncomfortable.

options.title: Let your body move
options.text: Walk around the room, shake out your hands, roll your shoulders.
options.why: Restlessness often eases a little when the body gets to move.

options.title: Tense and let go
options.text: Squeeze your hands and shoulders for a moment, then let them drop.
options.why: Tightening and then releasing can help restless energy settle.

acknowledge.text: Something is worrying you. You noticed it, and that helps.

options.title: Park the worry
options.text: Write the worry down and choose a time later to come back to it.
options.why: Many people find a set time for worrying makes it easier to let it rest in between.
options.prompt: What's worrying me (I'll come back to it later):

options.title: Yours, or not yours?
options.text: Which part of this can you do something about, and which part can you not?
options.why: Seeing what is in your hands can make the next step clearer.
options.prompt: What's in my hands here, and what isn't:

acknowledge.text: Something has got under your skin.

options.title: A longer out-breath
options.text: Breathe in gently, then breathe out a little longer, a few times.
options.why: Longer out-breaths can help the body cool down.

options.title: Name the itch
options.text: What exactly is irritating you? One line, no need to be fair.
options.why: Naming an irritation can make it smaller.

acknowledge.text: You're not convinced. That's allowed.

options.title: What would convince you?
options.text: What would you want to see or hear before feeling sure?
options.why: Knowing what is missing can turn doubt into a useful question.

options.title: Ask
options.text: If it helps, ask someone a clear question about what bothers you.
options.why: A direct question can often clear things up faster than wondering.

acknowledge.text: Things feel confusing right now. That can be unsettling.

options.title: Ground yourself first
options.text: Name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear.
options.why: Coming back to the present can make confusion feel less overwhelming.

options.title: One thing at a time
options.text: Write down what you do know, even if it is very little.
options.why: A small list of what is clear can be a place to start from.

acknowledge.text: You're not sure what to make of things. That's okay for now.

options.title: Untangle on paper
options.text: Write the question you are trying to answer, in one line.
options.why: A clear question is often easier to work on than a cloud of thoughts.
options.prompt: The question I'm trying to answer:

options.title: Talk it through
options.text: Explain it to someone you trust, out loud.
options.why: Saying something out loud can make it clearer.

acknowledge.text: You're seeing what's wrong. Sometimes that's useful, sometimes it's tiring.

options.title: Useful or heavy?
options.text: Is this criticism helping you change something, or just weighing on you?
options.why: Telling useful criticism from heavy criticism can make it easier to set down.
options.prompt: Is this helping me change something?

options.title: One kind thought
options.text: Find one thing that is going okay, alongside what is not.
options.why: A balanced view can make criticism easier to carry.

acknowledge.text: You want something for yourself. That's human.

options.title: What do you need?
options.text: What need is underneath this? Rest, space, attention?
options.why: Naming the need can help you meet it in a way you feel good about.

options.title: Meet it kindly
options.text: Find one small way to give yourself what you need today.
options.why: Looking after your needs is part of looking after others too.

acknowledge.text: Something felt awkward. That's a hard feeling, and a very common one.

options.title: Would they remember?
options.text: Would you think twice if someone else did this?
options.why: Many people judge themselves far more harshly than others would.

options.title: Let it pass through
options.text: A few slow breaths while the warmth fades.
options.why: Embarrassment often fades faster when we let it be there.

acknowledge.text: You feel silly about something. Be gentle with yourself.

options.title: Talk to yourself like a friend
options.text: What would you tell a friend who felt foolish about this?
options.why: Many of us are kinder to friends than to ourselves; this borrows that kindness.

options.title: What did you learn?
options.text: Is there anything useful to take from it?
options.why: A lesson can make an awkward moment feel worth something.
options.prompt: What I can take from it:

acknowledge.text: You're doubting yourself. Many people feel this, more often than they say.

options.title: Evidence for you
options.text: Write down three things you have handled well before.
options.why: Remembering what you have done can steady you when doubt is loud.

options.title: Write to yourself
options.text: Write to yourself for the next time you feel unsure.
options.why: Your own encouragement can be easier to believe later.

acknowledge.text: Something someone else has is pulling at you. That stings.

options.title: What does it point to?
options.text: What do you want that this jealousy is pointing to?
options.why: Jealousy often shows us something we care about.
options.prompt: What I want that this points to:

options.title: One small step
options.text: Take one small step towards that thing for yourself.
options.why: Turning a wish into a step can ease the sting.

acknowledge.text: Things are not going the way you want. That is frustrating.

options.title: Step away briefly
options.text: Leave it for a few moments: a walk, a drink of water, a stretch.
options.why: A short break can make a stuck thing easier to come back to.

options.title: Change one thing
options.text: What is one small thing you could try differently?
options.why: A small change can often get things moving again.
options.prompt: One thing I could try differently:

acknowledge.text: There is a lot on you right now.

options.title: Breathe out longer
options.text: Breathe in gently, and let the out-breath be longer, for a few rounds.
options.why: Longer out-breaths can help the body ease out of alert mode.

options.title: Empty your head
options.text: List everything on your mind, then circle just one thing to do next.
options.why: Getting it all down can make it feel more manageable.
options.prompt: Everything on my mind (then circle one):

acknowledge.text: It's all a bit much right now. You don't have to deal with all of it at once.

options.title: Ground yourself
options.text: Name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear.
options.why: Bringing attention to the present can make things feel more manageable.

options.title: Just the next thing
options.text: What is the one next small thing? Only that.
options.why: Shrinking the task to one step can make it possible again.

acknowledge.text: Anxiety is here. It's uncomfortable, and it can ease.

options.title: Slow your breathing
options.text: Follow the circle: in gently, out slowly.
options.why: Slow, longer out-breaths often help the body calm its alarm.

options.title: Five things you can see
options.text: Look around and name what you can see, touch and hear.
options.why: Grounding in the present can give anxious thoughts less to hold on to.

acknowledge.text: You are angry. Anger often means something mattered to you.

options.title: Let the heat out safely
options.text: Walk briskly, or squeeze and release your fists a few times.
options.why: Moving can help angry energy go somewhere safe.

options.title: What mattered?
options.text: What was crossed or not respected?
options.why: Knowing what anger is protecting can help you decide what to do.

acknowledge.text: You feel on guard against someone. That is a heavy way to feel.

options.title: Some space first
options.text: Step back from the situation if you can, and breathe slowly.
options.why: Distance and a calmer body can make the next choice clearer.

options.title: What happened?
options.text: What led to feeling this way? Just the facts, if you can.
options.why: Writing the facts down can help separate what happened from how it felt.

acknowledge.text: This is a very strong feeling. You can feel it without acting on it.

options.title: Slow everything down
options.text: Breathe slowly and put some distance between you and the situation.
options.why: A slower body often makes room for a calmer choice.

options.title: Talk to someone
options.text: If it feels like too much, talk to someone you trust, or a support line.
options.why: You do not have to hold a feeling this strong on your own.

acknowledge.text: You're furious. Let's get through the next little while safely.

options.title: Move it out
options.text: A brisk walk, or tense and release your arms and shoulders.
options.why: Moving can help strong anger burn off a little.

options.title: Breathe out longer
options.text: In gently, out longer, a few times.
options.why: Longer out-breaths can help the body calm down from high alert.

acknowledge.text: This is a lot of anger. Safety first, for you and for others.

options.title: Step away and breathe
options.text: If you can, move away from the situation and breathe out slowly.
options.why: Distance and slow breathing can help the strongest anger ease.

options.title: Talk to someone now
options.text: If you feel you might hurt someone or yourself, reach out now.
options.why: Support is there for moments exactly like this.
